source.title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
source.authors: Sonia Joseph; Praneet Suresh; E. Gol'dfarb; Lorenz Hufe; Yossi Gandelsman; Robert Graham; D. Bzdok; W. Samek; Blake Richards

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE decompositions to steer CLIP and improve task performance, but does not test the claim that sparse features are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures SAE sparsity and feature steerability in CLIP, a vision model rather than an LLM, so these findings do not test V4 as worded. It does not test superposition geometry, capacity competition, feature stability/completeness, or feature dimensionality. Downstream disentanglement and typographic-attack scores are omitted because they report task performance, not those representational claims.
record.test_reason: The paper trains SAEs on CLIP-ViT-B-32 and uses them as a tool for steering and disentanglement. It reports SAE sparsity, steerability and task accuracy, not tests of superposition. V4 names LLMs, and CLIP's vision encoder is not one. Nothing addresses toy geometry, capacity, alternative causes of polysemanticity, feature canonicity or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that CLIP vision SAEs show token- and layer-dependent sparsity unlike language SAEs. They also conclude that 10-15% of deeper-layer features are steerable with about 10x the concept coverage of neurons, and that SAE feature suppression improves CelebA and Waterbirds disentanglement and typographic-attack defense, with state-of-the-art results on PAINT.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains SAEs on CLIP vision-transformer activations and measures steering and downstream task performance; it does not reproduce the toy-network feature-overlap experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported properties vary by token type and patch position; the CLS sparsity pattern changes around layers 6-7, and steerability comparisons are reported for layer 11.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE L0 in CLIP varies by token type and patch position. Spatial-token L0 is reported as 3-14x that of external GPT-2 SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CLIP-ViT-B-32, SAE sparsity depends on token type, spatial position and layer, and is lower than for language-model SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: About 10-15% of layer-11 SAE features are steerable. SAE steering covers about 11% of vocabulary concepts versus about 1% for neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CLIP-ViT-B-32, SAE features give more steerable concept coverage than base neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-activating images are described as polysemantic for base neurons and task-specific for SAE features (Figure 2, Figure 10). This is qualitative, with no rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a vision transformer, SAE features are more monosemantic than neurons (would bear on a V4-like claim if extended beyond LLMs).

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted to the CVPR 2025 Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability for Vision (MIV)
record.problems: The representational results are from CLIP-ViT-B-32 and do not directly test superposition geometry. The layer-11 steerability analysis uses a subset of 12,000 features out of 49,152, and the steering metric depends on a 5,000-word vocabulary. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported results.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream CelebA, Waterbirds, and typographic-attack performance results are not included because they measure task outcomes rather than superposition, feature geometry, or feature recovery as specified by the claim.

untested.parts: No toy models, overlap geometry, sparsity transition or geometric structure.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
The study is on a vision transformer, not LLMs. SAE recoverability in CLIP is shown only as tool performance (appendix reconstruction metrics, qualitative top-activating images).
No completeness, stability or canonicity test of SAE features.
No test of one- vs multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: SAE reconstruction metrics per layer: explained variance about 0.68-0.99 and CE recovered about 90-100%. Relevant only if V4 is broadened to vision models.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition only as motivation for neuron polysemanticity. The polysemantic-neuron vs monosemantic-SAE-feature contrast is qualitative, based on maximally activating images. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network superposition, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry is tested.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The paper studies CLIP's vision transformer, not LLMs; it does not test the stated LLM claim.
No completeness, stability, or canonical-unit test of SAE features is reported.
The study represents SAE features as vectors but does not test whether model features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B-32
rows.operation_detail: Measured L0, the number of active SAE features per spatial token.
rows.note: The paper describes spatial-token L0 values as high; this measures SAE activation counts, not overlap geometry.
rows.check: Figure 4 shows a Layer 0 x64 vanilla SAE, so that condition should be stated instead of 'not specified'. This is SAE L0, not a superposition measure.

rows.operation_detail: Measured L0 patterns for the CLS token across layers.
rows.value: Transitions from sparse to rich representations around layers 6-7
rows.note: Qualitative description; the paper distinguishes CLS-token behavior from spatial-token behavior.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B-32
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE L0 values for CLIP and GPT-2 representations.

conditions.value: CLIP spatial tokens versus GPT-2 tokens

rows.value: CLIP spatial tokens have 3-14x higher activation counts
rows.note: The GPT-2 L0 values were collected from open-source SAEs, as stated in Appendix 9.
rows.check: The GPT-2 baseline (L0 20-50) comes from external open-source SAEs (Bloom), not the study's own measurement. The 3-14x figure compares across SAE training choices.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B-32
rows.operation_detail: Replaced a selected SAE feature's activation across all patches with steering strength 150.
rows.value: 1,322 of 12,000; approximately 100 are described as perfectly steerable
rows.note: The paper reports this as a steerability result, not as evidence about spontaneous feature overlap.
rows.check: This is a steerability count for the study's own metric. It is not a rate of a superposition-related property.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B-32
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept coverage from steering SAE features with coverage from steering neurons.
rows.baseline: Neuron steering accessed about 1% of concepts, about 50
rows.value: Feature steering accessed approximately 11% of concepts, about 550
rows.note: Coverage is defined by the paper's steerability threshold; it is not a direct measure of representational geometry.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (SAE steering vs neuron steering) on concept coverage. Figure 7 reports this per layer, and the row gives layer 11 only.
